marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q001.takeaway: Heme is protoporphyrin IX complexed with ferrous iron.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q001.displayText: Heme is ferroprotoporphyrin: ferrous iron (Fe2+) coordinated within protoporphyrin IX. Porphyrins are cyclic tetrapyrroles made of four pyrrole rings linked by methine bridges. In the source classification, uroporphyrin is the most water-soluble, coproporphyrin is intermediate, and protoporphyrin is least water-soluble.

rationales.b: Uroporphyrin is an intermediate in heme synthesis and is highly water-soluble, but the completed heme porphyrin ring is protoporphyrin IX.
rationales.c: Coproporphyrinogen precedes protoporphyrinogen in the pathway; coproporphyrin is not the porphyrin bound to iron in heme.
rationales.d: Benzoporphyrin is not the porphyrin ring used to form physiological heme.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q002.takeaway: Heme synthesis occurs in erythroid precursors and hepatocytes, but mature erythrocytes cannot synthesize heme.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q002.displayText: Heme synthesis is most active in erythroid precursors of bone marrow (about 85% of total synthesis in the source account) and in hepatocytes. The pathway alternates between mitochondria and cytosol: ALA synthase catalyzes the initial reaction in mitochondria, intermediate reactions occur in the cytosol, and the final steps return to mitochondria. Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and cannot synthesize heme.

rationales.a: Osteocytes are not a major heme-synthesis tissue; the source instead identifies erythroid precursors and hepatocytes as the principal sites.
rationales.b: Hepatocytes synthesize heme for cytochromes and other hemoproteins, so liver is a site of heme biosynthesis.
rationales.c: Erythroid precursors require abundant heme for hemoglobin and account for most heme production; they are a major synthesis site.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q003.takeaway: Mitochondrial succinyl-CoA combines with glycine to initiate heme synthesis.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q003.displayText: Heme synthesis begins in mitochondria when succinyl-CoA from the TCA cycle condenses with glycine. Pyridoxal-phosphate-dependent ALA synthase first forms α-amino-β-ketoadipate, which is rapidly decarboxylated to δ-aminolevulinate (ALA). Thus succinyl-CoA links the TCA cycle to porphyrin synthesis. The source pathway diagram remains the authority for the full sequence.

rationales.a: α-Ketoglutarate is a TCA intermediate, but the committed first substrate for heme synthesis is succinyl-CoA paired with glycine.
rationales.b: Fumarate is formed later in the TCA cycle and is not used by ALA synthase to initiate heme synthesis.
rationales.d: Malate is a TCA-cycle intermediate but is not the carbon donor used in the first reaction of porphyrin synthesis.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q004.takeaway: ALA synthase requires pyridoxal phosphate to condense glycine with succinyl-CoA at pathway entry.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q004.displayText: Mitochondrial ALA synthase (ALAS) uses pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) to catalyze the first reaction of heme biosynthesis: glycine condenses with succinyl-CoA to form α-amino-β-ketoadipate, which is then decarboxylated to δ-aminolevulinate (ALA). PLP supports the amino-acid chemistry of this reaction. The source's combined option describes the initial succinyl-CoA-to-α-amino-β-ketoadipate step.

rationales.b: The α-amino-β-ketoadipate intermediate is decarboxylated within the ALA-synthase reaction sequence; the defining PLP-dependent substrate-condensation step is the initial glycine–succinyl-CoA reaction.
rationales.c: ALA dehydratase condenses two ALA molecules to porphobilinogen; it is downstream and does not use PLP as the cofactor tested here.
rationales.d: Hydroxymethylbilane synthase polymerizes porphobilinogen units; this later cytosolic step is not PLP-dependent.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q005.takeaway: Hepatic ALAS1 is the rate-limiting enzyme of heme synthesis and is feedback-inhibited by heme.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q005.displayText: The rate-limiting step in hepatic heme synthesis is catalyzed by mitochondrial ALA synthase 1 (ALAS1), which forms ALA from glycine and succinyl-CoA. Heme exerts negative feedback on hepatic ALAS1 expression and activity. Drugs that induce hepatic cytochrome P450 increase heme use and can lower the regulatory heme pool, allowing ALAS1 induction. Erythroid ALAS2 is separately regulated by iron availability and erythroid demand.
emphasis: forms ALA from glycine and succinyl-CoA

rationales.b: Uroporphyrinogen III synthase cyclizes hydroxymethylbilane downstream in the pathway; it is not the rate-limiting enzyme in hepatic heme synthesis.
rationales.c: ALA dehydratase converts ALA to porphobilinogen and is inhibited by lead, but hepatic pathway regulation is chiefly at ALAS1.
rationales.d: Ferrochelatase inserts ferrous iron into protoporphyrin IX in the final step; it is not the rate-limiting hepatic enzyme.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q006.takeaway: Barbiturates induce CYP450, consume hepatic heme and derepress ALAS1, potentially triggering an acute porphyria attack.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q006.displayText: Barbiturates induce hepatic microsomal cytochrome P450, a heme-containing drug-metabolizing system. Increased heme use lowers the regulatory hepatic heme pool; reduced heme feedback then derepresses ALAS1, increasing ALA and other heme-pathway precursors. In acute intermittent porphyria, the downstream pathway is impaired, so precursor accumulation can precipitate a neurovisceral attack. Avoidance of porphyrinogenic drugs is therefore important in acute hepatic porphyrias.
emphasis: lowers the regulatory hepatic heme pool

rationales.a: Barbiturates reduce heme-mediated repression of ALAS1, so they derepress the enzyme; they do not repress its synthesis.
rationales.c: Ferrochelatase inhibition is classically associated with lead toxicity and protoporphyrin accumulation, not the CYP450-induction mechanism of barbiturates.
rationales.d: The keyed mechanism is a recognized trigger in acute intermittent porphyria; the vignette and source both specify ALAS derepression.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q007.takeaway: Lead poisoning inhibits ALA dehydratase, causing ALA and protoporphyrin accumulation.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q007.displayText: Ingestion of lead-based paint can cause abdominal pain and peripheral neuropathy. Lead inhibits heme synthesis, especially ALA dehydratase (porphobilinogen synthase), so ALA accumulates; it can also inhibit ferrochelatase, increasing protoporphyrin. The keyed enzyme is ALA dehydratase because it is the stronger diagnostic block in this question. Lead also disrupts heme-dependent enzymes and neuronal function.

rationales.a: ALA synthase catalyzes the first mitochondrial step from glycine and succinyl-CoA; lead primarily inhibits later enzymes rather than ALAS.
rationales.c: Heme synthase (ferrochelatase) is also inhibited by lead, but ALA dehydratase is the specific keyed defect and a major site of lead inhibition.
rationales.d: Coproporphyrinogen oxidase deficiency causes hereditary coproporphyria; it does not explain paint ingestion and the characteristic lead-inhibited ALA step.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q008.takeaway: Hydroxymethylbilane synthase releases ammonia while assembling four porphobilinogen units into hydroxymethylbilane.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q008.displayText: Cytosolic hydroxymethylbilane synthase (also called porphobilinogen deaminase) links four porphobilinogen molecules to form hydroxymethylbilane. Deamination releases four molecules of ammonia (NH3). Hydroxymethylbilane is then cyclized by uroporphyrinogen III synthase to enter the type III porphyrin pathway; spontaneous cyclization can instead yield type I products.

rationales.a: Water is involved in pathway chemistry, but the characteristic coproduct released as four porphobilinogen units are deaminated is ammonia.
rationales.c: Carbon dioxide is released during decarboxylation reactions, including ALA formation and later porphyrinogen processing, not during HMB-synthase polymerization.
rationales.d: CoA-SH is released when succinyl-CoA is used by ALA synthase at pathway entry; it is not produced by cytosolic HMB synthase.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q009.takeaway: Uroporphyrinogen III synthase cyclizes hydroxymethylbilane into the physiologic type III porphyrin precursor.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q009.displayText: Hydroxymethylbilane is normally cyclized by uroporphyrinogen III synthase to form uroporphyrinogen III, the first cyclic porphyrinogen in heme synthesis. In the absence of the synthase, hydroxymethylbilane can cyclize spontaneously to uroporphyrinogen I, a nonphysiologic type I isomer. The distinction is important in congenital erythropoietic porphyria, where deficient enzyme activity favors type I porphyrins.

rationales.a: Uroporphyrinogen I is the spontaneous type I product when cyclization is not directed by the type III synthase; it is not the enzyme that catalyzes physiologic cyclization.
rationales.b: There is no relevant uroporphyrinogen II synthase in the canonical pathway; the source-keyed enzyme is uroporphyrinogen III synthase.
rationales.d: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase acts later, removing carboxyl groups from uroporphyrinogen to form coproporphyrinogen.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q010.takeaway: Erythropoietic protoporphyria is usually autosomal recessive, unlike the commonly autosomal-dominant hepatic porphyrias listed.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q010.displayText: The source classifies erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) as autosomal recessive and associates it with reduced ferrochelatase (FECH) activity. It is a common porphyria of children, who classically develop nonblistering photosensitivity. An increased ratio of free to zinc-bound protoporphyrin in erythrocytes is a hallmark, and diagnosis can be supported by FECH mutation analysis. Many hepatic porphyrias, including acute intermittent, hereditary coproporphyria and variegate porphyria, are autosomal dominant. EPP inheritance can be more complex because many patients have a FECH variant together with a low-expression allele; the source's exam contrast remains that EPP is not the dominant choice.

rationales.b: Variegate porphyria is generally autosomal dominant and can produce both acute neurovisceral attacks and cutaneous photosensitivity.
rationales.c: Acute intermittent porphyria is an autosomal-dominant hepatic porphyria caused by HMBS deficiency, with variable penetrance.
rationales.d: Hereditary coproporphyria is usually autosomal dominant and results from coproporphyrinogen oxidase deficiency.
